lesson.title: X, Y, and the Coin Flip: How Sex Is Determined
lesson.summary: In humans, one pair of chromosomes out of twenty three, the X and Y sex chromosomes, determines whether an embryo develops as male or female, and it is the father's sperm that decides the outcome.
lesson.body:
Humans are diploid, carrying forty six chromosomes arranged in twenty three pairs, while gametes, sperm and eggs, are haploid, carrying just twenty three chromosomes, one from each pair. Twenty two of those twenty three pairs are autosomes, chromosomes that look the same in both sexes and carry genes for traits unrelated to sex. The twenty third pair is different: it is the pair of sex chromosomes, and which combination an individual carries determines biological sex.

A typical female carries two X chromosomes, XX. A typical male carries one X chromosome and one Y chromosome, XY. Because a female's two sex chromosomes are both X, every egg cell she produces during meiosis carries a single X chromosome, there is no other option. Because a male carries one X and one Y, his sperm cells split into two types partway through meiosis, with roughly half carrying an X chromosome and half carrying a Y chromosome.

Fertilization is what actually sets the outcome. An egg, which always carries an X, can be fertilized by either an X bearing sperm or a Y bearing sperm. If an X bearing sperm fertilizes the egg, the resulting embryo is XX and typically develops as female. If a Y bearing sperm fertilizes the egg, the resulting embryo is XY and typically develops as male. Since the two types of sperm are produced in roughly equal numbers, each fertilization is close to a fifty fifty coin flip, and it is technically the father's sperm, not the mother's egg, that determines the outcome. A gene located on the Y chromosome, called SRY, triggers the developmental cascade toward testes early in an XY embryo, while its absence in an XX embryo allows female development to proceed by default.

This sets up the next chapter directly. Because genes are physically carried on chromosomes, any gene that happens to sit on the X or the Y chromosome will be inherited following this same predictable XX and XY pattern, rather than the ordinary autosomal pattern seen in every cross up to this point. Genes that live on the sex chromosomes are called sex-linked, and they behave differently enough to deserve their own set of rules.
